items.title: Reference Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) technology has revolutionized the digital marketing sector, yet its impact on consumer psychology requires deeper understanding. Employing a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach based on the Scopus database, this study analyzes the relationships among GenAI usage, customer engagement, and customer trust. Literature mapping reveals that current research focuses on four primary clusters: consumer behavioral dynamics and purchase intentions, visual quality (hyperrealism), transparency and ethical issues, and collaborative creativity efficiency. Based on an analysis of these findings, the study identifies an "Authenticity Paradox," wherein AI-generated hyperrealistic visuals effectively boost purchase intentions but risk triggering the "uncanny valley" effect thereby undermining consumer trust if transparency is lacking. Trust is significantly shaped by the interplay between drivers, such as transparent labeling (watermarking), and inhibitors, such as visual artifacts and privacy concerns. Regarding engagement effectiveness, AI proves superior in stimulating interaction among existing followers, whereas human-generated content remains essential for reaching new audiences due to its empathy and emotional resonance. The study concludes that adopting a hybrid marketing strategy specifically Human-AI Co-Creation represents the optimal approach for synergizing GenAI's technological efficiency with the authenticity of the human touch in the long term.

items.title: Reflections on the management of literary works with educational content for the development of the personality of university students
items.abstract: The education of university students requires strategies that link literary reading with personality development. Objective: To present reflections on the management of literary works with educational content for the personality development of university students, based on articles from partner journals—the Cuban Journal of Information Sciences in Health and Islands—located with the support of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and compared with academic literature. Methodology: A qualitative, descriptive-propositive approach was adopted. The proposal was evaluated through consultation with eight professionals in the educational field, including teachers and administrators, intentionally selected for their experience in higher education, reading promotion, and academic management. Results: The reflections were organized into four dimensions: reading and educational diagnosis, selection of works with educational content, planning and allocation of resources, and evaluation of educational outcomes. The proposal highlights the need to coordinate libraries, faculty, and administrative teams to promote reading practices linked to values, empathy, self-esteem, and critical thinking. Conclusion/Contributions: The educational management of literary works can contribute to the development of university students' personalities when accompanied by clear objectives, teacher guidance, administrator participation, and periodic evaluation.

items.title: Reforming General Academic English: a public-health-themed curriculum for Chinese medical students
items.abstract: Public health is an interdisciplinary system that integrates natural science, social practice, and humanistic concepts, committed to safeguarding the population-wide health of society. The global public health crisis triggered by COVID-19 has further pushed public health education into a core position of higher medical education, and integrating public health perspectives into general courses has become a critical trend of disciplinary integration. As a transitional bridge connecting general English and medical English for Specific Purposes (ESP), General Academic English (GAE) at Shandong Medical and Pharmaceutical University (SDMPU) undertakes multiple educational missions: improving students' academic English literacy, fostering autonomous learning competence (1), and meeting national talent cultivation requirements that emphasize humanistic awareness, global vision and international communication capabilities (2).Integrating public health themes into GAE serves as a targeted curriculum optimization approach, which effectively bridges medical humanities and public health expertise, and responds to China's New Liberal Arts initiative launched in 2019 (3). The initiative aims to break traditional disciplinary boundaries and promote interdisciplinary thinking to cultivate high-level compound medical talents.After years of iterative teaching practice, the public-health-themed GAE curriculum at SDMPU has formed preliminary interdisciplinary features. Nevertheless, reflective curriculum analysis indicates that the current teaching arrangement still fails to fully achieve the intended interdisciplinary educational goals. Multiple structural, organizational and practical limitations constrain the curriculum's interdisciplinary cultivation effects. Based on long-term front-line teaching observations and a systematic review of relevant domestic and international studies on medical academic English and public health pedagogy, this paper argues that targeted curriculum reconstruction is necessary to better align GAE instruction with contemporary educational demands, and the institutional talent training positioning. The public-health-themed GAE course examined herein is a 1.5-credit elective offered in the fourth semester for second-year undergraduate Clinical Medicine (Bachelor of Medicine -5-year program) students. Cohorts for this elective typically include approximately 700 students. The course is coordinated by one dedicated overall coordinator and delivered by five English instructors with academic backgrounds in linguistics or literature, each permanently assigned to a fixed teaching chapter; no public-health specialists participate on a regular basis. The course comprises 32 wholeclass in-person lecture hours throughout the semester; small-group activities are embedded within lecture sessions, with no separate dedicated tutorial time, and self-paced pre-class MOOC materials are assigned as out-of-class preparation and are therefore excluded from the 32 contact hours.Assessment consists of one formal final examination weighting 60% and continuous assessment weighting 40%; within the continuous component, group assignments account for 20% and individual assignments for 80%. Core thematic coverage encompasses health governance, nutritional health, genetics, mental health, and traditional Chinese medicine. A concise overview of key programmatic features is provided in Table 1 for cross-institutional reference.This opinion article builds its curriculum reform arguments upon three interrelated theoretical and policy foundations: ESP curriculum design principles, the interdisciplinary philosophy of China's New Liberal Arts initiative, and community-centered perspectives in public health education. In addition, it adopts a normative analytical approach guided by Kern's six-step curriculum development framework.First, ESP principles advocate the integration of language skill training and disciplinary content learning, focusing on context-specific professional communicative needs rather than generalized language instruction (4). Second, the New Liberal Arts initiative promotes cross-disciplinary integration to cultivate compound talents capable of coping with complex social and public health challenges (5). Third, community-centered public health education emphasizes scenario-based practice and real-world problem-solving, encouraging classroom knowledge transfer into authentic community health contexts (6). To clarify, this opinion article analyses an existing course for iterative improvement instead of presenting a de-novo full-cycle curriculum-development project. We therefore treat Kern's framework as an informing reference rather than the strict organisational backbone of the manuscript.We adopt the current structure (curriculum characteristics-dilemmas-reconstruction pathways), which better fits our analytical focus on describing the course status quo and diagnosing implementationrelated challenges. Key elements from Kern's steps are discussed across corresponding sections, while full iterative execution of the six-step cycle is reserved for future practical curriculum delivery.Beyond these overarching foundations, three supplementary analytical lenses are adopted for targeted analysis in subsequent sections. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) provides a framework to examine learner motivation and barriers to engagement. The Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework guides the design of AI-enhanced interactive learning activities. Programmatic Assessment underpins the multi-stakeholder, process-oriented evaluation system proposed for curriculum reconstruction. These three lenses serve as specialised analytical tools embedded within the broader Kern-guided curriculum analysis. The interrelationships among these theoretical foundations and analytical lenses are visualised in Figure 1. The characteristics outlined in this section describe the intended formal curriculum design of the public-health-themed GAE course, representing its structural and thematic aspirations. This section addresses four core attributes: interdisciplinary integration, popular science-oriented curriculum design, diversified blended learning arrangements, and cultivation of cross-cultural critical thinking.Nevertheless, gaps remain between curricular design intentions and day-to-day instructional delivery;these practical implementation challenges are analysed further in Section 4.The public health-oriented GAE curriculum transcends the narrow boundaries of conventional language teaching and integrates interdisciplinary knowledge across public health, clinical nutrition, basic medical sciences, genetics, psychology and medical humanities. Different from general English courses that focus merely on linguistic competence, this interdisciplinary embedding enriches students' systematic knowledge of public health and fosters their multidimensional cross-disciplinary thinking, enabling learners to interpret medical and public health issues from multiple perspectives beyond pure language acquisition.The textbook system of this GAE course at SDMPU takes public health popularization as the main thread throughout curriculum design. It covers a wide range of authentic and practical public health themes, including disciplinary origin debates, cutting-edge medical technologies, and prevalent public health challenges such as dietary-related diseases, nutritional imbalance, and mental health disorders. Key professional public health vocabulary is annotated and interpreted in the textbook, taking into account the dual attributes of language foundation and popular science dissemination.This design aligns with the positioning of GAE as a transitional bridge course between general English and specialized medical English.In terms of teaching organization and implementation, the GAE course adopts an online-offline blended learning model supported by a professional MOOC platform, which realizes full-cycle teaching design covering pre-class preview, in-class thematic expansion, and after-class knowledge consolidation. The course is jointly delivered by a professional teaching team, who adopt differentiated and diversified instructional strategies according to different thematic chapters.Multiple teaching forms, including traditional classroom lectures, flipped classroom tasks, thematic group presentations, and collaborative academic workshops, are flexibly applied in teaching practice.Such diversified blended learning designs seek to enrich classroom teaching scenarios, stimulate students' learning initiative, and enhance learners' proficiency in public health English.In curriculum content arrangement, comparative reading materials are adopted to trigger critical thinking regarding transnational public health governance. For example, thematically paired English texts concerning Chinese and American healthcare systems are introduced in routine teaching. Such comparative reading enables medical students to intuitively analyze institutional differences in public health governance across countries, reflect on the practical dilemmas and optimization directions in global public health development, and integrate linguistic training with humanistic and international public health cognition. This instructional design helps students avoid simplistic, stereotyped perceptions of global public health issues and gradually develop objective, critical and globalized public health literacy. These comparative reading activities aim to foster students' intercultural communicative competence (9) and cultural humility (10), which constitute core dimensions of established global health competency frameworks. Beyond improving basic academic language proficiency, such comparative materials encourage medical students to recognize diversified international public health contexts, embrace cross-cultural differences, and build global-minded perspectives for future professional cross-cultural health communication.While the GAE course possesses promising design-related characteristics laid out in Section 3, gaps between formal curriculum intentions and practical instructional delivery give rise to multiple implementation-level dilemmas that restrict the expected interdisciplinary teaching effectiveness.This section examines these practical challenges across four dimensions: insufficient learning and teaching motivation, fragmented team teaching and overloaded group assignments, disjointed blended learning, and limited social practice opportunities.At SDMPU, General Academic English is set as an elective course, which brings structural challenges for learning motivation. As documented in existing pedagogical studies (11), electivecourse status may shape learners' course-selection priorities. From the authors' front-line teaching observations, some students may prioritize credit completion when selecting electives and may allocate comparatively less time and energy to GAE compared with compulsory medical majors, with superficial engagement in homework and classroom tasks observable among a subset of learners.This practical concern resonates with the core argument from SDT, which highlights how contextual factors and motivational regulation shape learners' perceived autonomy and quality of engagement (12). The elective attribute may also create challenges for consistent teaching standards. Formative evaluation relies heavily on group assignments lacking standardized supervision mechanisms. Based on the authors' teaching observations together with published literature, free-riding behaviors can occasionally emerge within learning teams (13), which may reduce the expected training benefits of collaborative tasks.The rotational team teaching model, in which different instructors are responsible for separate chapters, may bring notable practical trade-offs despite diversifying classroom practice. From the authors' front-line teaching observations, frequent instructor handovers can lead to fractured logical coherence across chapters and inconsistent instructional rhythms, imposing ongoing adaptation pressure on students exposed to divergent teaching styles. Meanwhile, over-reliance on group assignments may add substantial workload for medical students, who are already occupied by intensive professional coursework. As also highlighted in existing relevant literature (13), poorly designed group-based tasks may create conditions raising potential risks of academic misconduct including plagiarism of group assignments.Although flipped classroom and MOOC resources are formally incorporated, the overall teaching logic still leans toward traditional offline lecture-centered models, which may limit the complementary value of online resources. Common practical problems include outdated, lowmatching MOOC materials disconnected from classroom themes, and most instructors take offline teaching as the absolute core while online resources only serve as superficial add-ons without systematic integrated design (14). The separation of online knowledge input and offline practical training can render the blended-learning framework partially nominal in practice.Public health education emphasizes community participation and real-scene problem-solving, enabling students to apply disciplinary vocabulary and logical thinking to solve real social health challenges (15). However, constrained by traditional classroom-centered teaching concepts, the practical activities of the current GAE course at SDMPU are limited to campus-based tasks such as poster design. There is a lack of extended off-campus social practice targeting community residents, foreigners and public health service institutions. The disconnection between classroom theoretical learning and real public health scenarios may create a notable gap between curriculum design goals and practical teaching outcomes. To achieve these learning objectives, curriculum content can be enriched with interdisciplinary resources. Rooted in the multi-dimensional integration logic of public health education covering biomedicine, social science, environmental governance and medical ethics (16), GAE may seek to expand curriculum content with cross-domain resources such as medical resource allocation, occupational health and environmental public health, and embed historical humanistic materials to enrich thematic depth.Two core transformation directions may be identified in curriculum positioning: shifting from single discipline-oriented language training to social demand-oriented interdisciplinary talent cultivation (17), and integrating ideological and political education throughout all thematic modules. Teachers can design diversified off-campus practical activities closely linked to public health themes:producing English popular science videos, delivering community public health lectures, participating in Model United Nations debates on global health, and surveying the application of English public health signs in local medical institutions. These practices may help strengthen medical students' social responsibility and support the fundamental educational goal of fostering virtue through teaching (18,19).As a fundamental institutional guarantee for constructing a stable interdisciplinary blended learning system, SDMPU may consider upgrading GAE to a compulsory course to mitigate motivational deficits originating from the elective-course positioning. Such institutional adjustment may elevate the course's institutional status, help raise students' awareness of the course, and enhance instructors' teaching dedication. With improved curriculum positioning, both students and teaching staff may maintain more sustained and effective engagement, helping lay a solid institutional foundation for standardized, high-quality interdisciplinary blended teaching and public health English training.To address instructional fragmentation caused by frequent instructor handovers in rotational team teaching, SDMPU may establish a fixed core teaching team to unify instructional logic, textbook standards and assessment requirements, thereby reducing repeated adaptation burdens for students. In response to the interdisciplinary requirements of the New Liberal Arts initiative, medical English instructors and clinical and public health specialists can form long-term collaborative teaching communities. Professional physicians deliver instruction on core public health thematic knowledge, while language instructors focus on academic expression, poster composition and international communication skills. Drawing on mature interdisciplinary teaching practices from Capital Medical University (20), this dual-instructor collaborative model may support both professional accuracy and satisfactory language training outcomes (21).To restructure the nominal blended-learning model, the proposed curriculum adopts a project-driven blended-learning design grounded in the CoI framework, which conceptualizes effective onlineoffline education through three interrelated presences: teaching presence, social presence, and cognitive presence (22). Within the GAE curriculum, pre-class MOOC learning supports individual knowledge acquisition; in-class project-oriented, public-health-themed tasks foster peer interaction and collaborative inquiry, while targeted instructor guidance sustains coherent teaching presence throughout the whole learning cycle.The blended learning system realizes rational functional division and organic coordination between online and offline instructional links: online MOOC platforms support pre-class theoretical learning, case reading, and autonomous knowledge sorting (23), while offline classroom sessions focus on project-based practical tasks centered on authentic public health themes (24). Taking the "Diet andHealth" chapter as an example, instructors can design diversified group projects oriented to public health science communication (25). Specific tasks include producing bilingual health popular science videos (26), designing publicity posters for foreign-resident communities, and participating in themed international debate activities (27). To optimize learning outcomes, instructors may moderately adjust the proportion of group assignments and individual tasks to balance student workload. Such flexible arrangement helps alleviate excessive academic pressure on medical students and mitigate potential risks of superficial learning and academic misconduct. Through systematic online-offline integration and well-structured project design, students are able to apply academic English competencies in authentic public health communication scenarios, gradually cultivating the international communication capacity required for future participation in global health governance.Additionally, widely accessible generative AI translation tools bring new pedagogical considerations to this English teaching context. Although AI translation offers convenient linguistic support for medical students, over-reliance on machine translation may hinder vocabulary retention and the development of independent English expression (28). In this GAE curriculum, instructors may adopt balanced strategies: designing offline output tasks without translation tools, prioritizing active language production in authentic public health communication activities, and embedding guidance on proper AI tool use within teaching. These measures seek to frame AI as an auxiliary aid rather than a replacement for learners' language-skill development.Aligned with the blended learning arrangement, the curriculum evaluation system seeks to move beyond sole reliance on final examinations to establish a multi-dimensional evaluation mechanism.This multi-dimensional design aligns with the core spirit of programmatic assessment, which advocates continuous, holistic collection of learner evidence rather than high-stakes singleexamination outcomes (29). First, weights for online and offline assessments may be rationally allocated (30): online platforms leverage big data to record students' autonomous learning trajectories for formative assessment (31), while offline evaluation centers on classroom engagement, group project progress and practical performance. Second, targeted evaluation criteria may be developed for public health practice activities. Relevant references include mature indicator frameworks for medical popular science video assessment (32) and standardized English public signs in hospitals (33); alternatively, task-specific evaluation dimensions can be developed according to the features of each project task. Third, expand evaluation participants to form a five-dimensional evaluation matrix covering intelligent learning platforms, student self-assessment, instructor scoring, peer review, and social feedback from practice recipients. items.title: Reframing Anthropometry and Ergonomics Beyond the Normative Body
items.abstract: Within interior architecture education, anthropometry and ergonomics constitute foundational domains of knowledge for understanding the relationship between users and designed environments. Their pedagogical application often positions the user as a body to be measured, proportioned, and accommodated within space. This study recasts that initial framing by asking how these domains can be taught beyond the normative body and how they may support a relational understanding of user, action, object, and space. The study was conducted as part of an undergraduate course, Ergonomics in Interior Architecture, at Özyeğin University during the Fall 2024–2025 semester; through an active learning exercise structured around role-playing, a case study, and a poster session. The study was conducted in the Ergonomics in Interior Architecture course at Özyeğin University during the Fall 2024–2025 semester through an active learning exercise structured around role-playing, a case study, and a poster session. Students created fictional users with non-normative bodies, mapped their daily routines, and developed spatial and furniture proposals responsive to their abilities, limitations, and needs. The research material comprised the project posters and written reflections of 10 students who completed all stages of the exercise. The data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. The findings indicate that the students moved beyond the procedural application of anthropometric and ergonomic standards, interpreting bodily difference as a generator of design reasoning. The study suggests that by centering a non-normative user in a design problem, anthropometry and ergonomics can move beyond their conventional role as instruments of fit and become pedagogical means through which students learn to understand interior space as a relational field.

items.title: Regulating the Future of Surgery: A Comparative Global Review of Approval Pathways, Safety Standards, and Compliance for Robotic Surgical Systems: A Comprehensive Global Policy, Regulatory Framework, and Risk Assessment Review
items.abstract: Robotic Surgical Systems (RSS) have fundamentally transformed modern clinical therapeutics by enabling unprecedented precision, minimally invasive dexterity, and enhanced 3D visualization. However, the convergence of complex mechatronics, autonomous software algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and telesurgery presents unprecedented regulatory, ethical, and clinical risk profiles. This comprehensive review provides a rigorous comparative analysis of global approval pathways across four major jurisdictions: the United States (FDA), the European Union (EU MDR), Japan (PMDA), and India (CDSCO). We examine pre-market medical device classification, substantial equivalence standards, clinical evaluation requirements, cyber-security paradigms, post-market surveillance (PMS), and surgeon credentialing compliance. Furthermore, this paper critically addresses emerging regulatory hurdles surrounding generative AI integration, autonomous robotic navigation, liabilities in telesurgical latency, and data privacy frameworks. Recommendations are offered for establishing globally harmonized regulatory standards and adaptive oversight protocols to safe-guard patient safety while fostering technological innovation.

items.abstract: A representative transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement system illustrates a high-risk structural-heart technology that enables replacement of the native tricuspid valve without conventional open-heart surgery. A system of this kind typically integrates a bovine-pericardial valve, a self-expanding nitinol frame and anchoring architecture, and a transfemoral venous delivery platform. Such devices have received Breakthrough Device designation and subsequent Premarket Approval (PMA) in the United States for patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) despite optimal medical therapy when replacement is deemed appropriate by a heart team. This article reconstructs the generalized regulatory journey for this device category and integrates classification, standards, clinical evidence, market positioning, global harmonization, project management, regulatory risk, human factors, quality systems, and real-world evidence. An illustrative Gantt chart provides a realistic development model for a device of this risk class. items.title: Repositioning language centres and self-access centres in the age of Artificial Intelligence: From resource provision to human-centred mediation
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has unsettled established assumptions in language education. For University Language Centres (LCs) and Self-Access Language Centres (SALCs), AI systems offering instant feedback, writing support, language models, and conversational practice raise questions about their distinctive institutional roles. This opinion paper argues that LCs and SALCs should not compete with AI as providers of content or feedback. Instead, they should become human-centred mediating institutions that help learners, teachers, and institutions use AI critically, ethically, and pedagogically. After revisiting their established roles in supporting autonomous and self-directed language learning, the paper argues that AI demands a more cautious understanding of autonomy, as apparent independence may conceal overreliance, weak evaluative judgement, and outsourced cognition (Barrett & Pack, 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2024). It proposes five future functions of LCs and SALCs: AI literacy development, pedagogical curation, ethical mediation, reflective learner advising, and the integration of formal and informal learning. Drawing on the planned Language Education Institute at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, the paper illustrates how language policy, technology-enhanced pedagogy, and human-centred education may be aligned. Ultimately, the value of LCs and SALCs lies in cultivating judgement, agency, accountability, and community.

items.title: Research and Practice on the Construction of a Lightweight AI-Enabled Welding Experimental Teaching and Safety Intelligent Management System
items.abstract: Aiming at the four prominent problems existing in current multi-process welding laboratories, including difficult supervision of teaching processes, high pressure on safety risk prevention and control, fragmented integration of teaching and management, and difficult implementation of intelligent transformation, this paper takes an eight-category multi-process, multi-equipment, and multi-scene welding experimental teaching system as the research object. Adopting the methods of literature research, field investigation, pilot verification and closed-loop optimization, this study constructs an integrated intelligent management system with in-depth integration of teaching and safety, covering the whole experimental process of pre-class, in-class and after-class stages supported by lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Lightweight AI capabilities are deeply embedded in four key links: standardization of teaching procedures, standardization of operational behaviors, evaluability of experimental quality, and early warning of safety risks, forming a low-cost, easy-to-implement, replicable and scalable intelligent management paradigm for engineering experiments. Practical results show that the proposed system significantly improves the standardization, proceduralization and objectivity of welding experimental teaching, strengthens the capabilities of pre-event early warning, rapid disposal and closed-loop rectification of safety risks, and effectively reduces human supervision omissions. It provides a referable practical path for the digital transformation of university experimental teaching and the modernization of laboratory governance capacity.

items.title: Research on the Construction and Practice of AI Literacy Course
items.abstract: Amid rapid generative AI growth, cultivating AI literacy among non-computer science (non-CS) undergraduates is a key higher education reform priority. Drawing on national policies and domestic course experience, this study constructs a five-dimensional progressive AI literacy framework: fundamental knowledge, risk identification, safety awareness, ethical analysis, governance participation. Pedagogically, the course uses an online smart platform for multimodal delivery, case-based teaching, and integrated process-team assessment. In a teaching practice of AI Safety, Ethics, and Governance with 66 non-CS undergraduates (44 valid surveys), results show a moderate positive correlation between classroom interaction and team project quality; students highly value innovative assessments like team projects and self-designed questions, and most gain achievement from work selected as teaching cases. This study offers an empirically grounded, data-driven course design and evaluation framework, filling the general education gap for non-CS students.

items.title: ResearchMind AI An AI-Powered Multi-Domain Research Paper Analysis and Report Generation System
items.abstract: ResearchMind AI is an AI-powered system designed to simplify research paper analysis across multiple domains. It enables users to upload and analyze multiple research papers in PDF format. PyMuPDF is used to extract text, while Sentence Transformers generate semantic embeddings. ChromaDB stores and retrieves relevant information through semantic search. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is integrated with an open-source Large Language Model (LLM) to provide context-based answers. The system supports automated literature survey generation, research gap identification, paper comparison, and intelligent question answering. It also generates structured research reports summarizing key findings and future research directions. The application uses React.js for the frontend and Flask with Python for the backend. ResearchMind AI aims to reduce manual effort, improve research organization, and make literature analysis more efficient.

items.title: Resilience and Risk Management in Circular Supply Chains
items.abstract: Over the last decade, industrial systems have been shaken by overlapping crises such as climate change, pandemics, resource pressures, and geopolitical instability. In response, Industry 5.0 has moved beyond the automation-centered logic of Industry 4.0 by placing human well-being, sustainability, and resilience at the core of industrial value creation. In parallel, circular-economy thinking encourages firms to redesign supply chains around closed material loops, extended product lifetimes, and higher-value resource recovery. This chapter examines how Industry 5.0 and the circular economy can mutually reinforce each other when supported by digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, blockchain, and digital twins. Rather than being treated as purely technical add-ons, these technologies enable predictive risk management, real-time monitoring, improved traceability, and more adaptive supply-chain configurations. Drawing on illustrative cases from the automotive, electronics, fashion, food and beverage, and logistics sectors, the chapter demonstrates that human-centered governance is a key condition for translating digital and circular strategies into resilient supply-chain practices. It concludes by proposing a human-centric circular resilience framework that positions resilience and risk management as central mechanisms for sustainable resource valorization and outlines implications for policymakers, industrial practitioners, and researchers.

items.title: Resilience and work engagement: the mediating role of job crafting behaviours
items.abstract: Introduction Despite growing recognition that resilience and work engagement are central to employee wellbeing, the mechanisms through which resilience is associated with engaged work behaviour remain underexplored. Grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined task, cognitive, and relational job crafting as parallel mediating mechanisms in the resilience-work engagement relationship. Methods Cross-sectional data were collected from 332 employees at a large financial services organisation operating across South Africa and Namibia. Resilience, job crafting, and work engagement were assessed using validated measures. A parallel mediation model was tested using PROCESS macro Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Resilience significantly predicted all three crafting behaviours and work engagement. All indirect effects were statistically significant. Cognitive crafting showed the largest estimated indirect effect, followed by relational and task crafting. The model explained 34% of variance in work engagement, with crafting behaviours accounting for approximately 45% of the total effect of resilience on engagement. The direct effect remained significant, indicating partial mediation. Discussion Resilient employees actively reshape their work through behavioural, cognitive, and relational crafting, and this proactive activity meaningfully explains how resilience generates engagement. Cognitive reframing of work as purposeful and meaningful emerged as the most potent pathway. Findings carry practical relevance for resilience training, leadership practice, and organisational job design.

items.title: Reversibility-Aware AI for Supply Chain Decision-Making: A Risk-Adaptive Framework for Human–AI Control
items.abstract: Background: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems move from supply chain decision support towards operational execution, governance must distinguish technical capability from permissible decision authority. This study develops a reversibility-aware framework for allocating human–AI control according to decision risk, recoverability, uncertainty and consequence propagation.Methods: A design science research-inspired approach was used to operationalise four constructs on normalised scales and integrate them into an equally weighted Decision Control Score (DCS), supplemented by governance overrides. Five control modes, from HC-0 (human-controlled) to HC-4 (monitored AI execution), were evaluated using six author-constructed supply chain scenarios. The framework was compared with illustrative fixed HC-3 and risk-only baselines, followed by reversibility and weighting sensitivity analyses.Results: The framework assigned HC-4 to routine inventory replenishment, HC-3 to forecast adjustment and purchase-order quantity modification, HC-2 to logistics rerouting, HC-1 to supplier selection or replacement, and HC-0 to critical supply interruption response. Its recommendations differed from the risk-only baseline in two of six scenarios. When the other constructs were held constant, varying reversibility changed the logistics-rerouting control mode. Across four alternative weighting configurations and six scenarios, 23 of 24 classifications matched the equal-weight results (95.8%).Conclusion: The analytical evaluation illustrates how recovery feasibility can affect rule-based control allocation. Because scenario inputs, weights, thresholds and safeguards were stipulated rather than empirically calibrated, these findings do not establish operational effectiveness or predictive validity. Independent expert assessment and field validation are required before implementation.

items.title: Review of Applications of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) in Water Resource Engineering
items.abstract: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have evolved from primarily cartographic and spatial-data management environments into core analytical infrastructure for water-resource engineering. Their application now spans watershed delineation, rainfall–runoff modelling, groundwater assessment, flood and drought analysis, irrigation planning, water-quality assessment, river management and water-distribution infrastructure. However, the literature is fragmented across application domains and frequently attributes the predictive capability of remote sensing, hydrological models or machine-learning algorithms to GIS itself. This review critically synthesizes the evidence contained in a 20-study working corpus and supplements it with recent peer-reviewed literature to identify how GIS contributes to water-resource engineering, where its contribution is strongest, and which methodological weaknesses continue to limit transferability and decision reliability. The review is organized around six application domains and evaluates the GIS role across data integration, terrain analysis, spatial modelling, decision support, visualization and model coupling. The synthesis shows a transition from conventional GIS-based watershed and groundwater mapping toward integrated workflows combining digital elevation models, satellite observations, hydrological/hydraulic models, geostatistics, artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Nevertheless, recurring weaknesses are evident: non-reproducible literature selection, inconsistent validation, inadequate uncertainty quantification, scale mismatch, dependence on subjective weighting in multi-criteria methods, insufficient benchmarking between GIS-enabled and non-GIS workflows, and geographical concentration of evidence.Recent systematic reviews reinforce these concerns, particularly the need for standardized validation and uncertainty protocols and for multi-source, physically informed modelling. The review therefore proposes a GIS–water-resource engineering framework in which GIS is treated not as the predictive model itself but as the spatial integration and decision-support layer connecting observations, process models, data-driven models and management actions. A research agenda is proposed around uncertainty-aware GIS, hybrid physics–AI modelling, cloud-native geospatial workflows, real-time sensor integration, digital twins, explainable AI and reproducible open science. The review provides a conceptual basis for researchers and practitioners to design more transparent, validated and decision-oriented GIS applications in water-resource engineering.

items.title: Revisiting Managerial Rationality: Structural Limitations of Agent-Based Artificial Intelligence in Executive Decision-Making
items.abstract: This paper examines the limitations of artificial intelligence–driven managerial rationality in top management, with a focus on agent-based AI models. This study employs a systematic literature review using a PRISMA-inspired approach to analyze agent-based AI models in executive decision-making contexts. Drawing on the contemporary scientific literature, the study conceptualizes AI as a probabilistic decision-support mechanism rather than an autonomous managerial actor. The paper identifies key structural and epistemic constraints of agent-based AI, including probabilistic outputs, bounded rationality, and contextual dependence, emphasizing the need for sustained human participation and oversight in executive decision-making.

items.title: Rigor, commitment, and generative AI: a conceptual framework for student engagement in EAP writing
items.abstract: The increasing integration of GenAI into academic writing has prompted renewed attention to how students engage with writing tasks in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) contexts. While existing research has focused on GenAI's capabilities and risks, it has paid less attention to the instructional conditions that shape how students use these tools. This paper proposes the Rigor–Commitment Alignment Framework (RCAF), a conceptual model that examines the interaction between academic rigor and teacher commitment as two dimensions of the pedagogical environment. Drawing on research in academic literacies, engagement theory, self-determination theory, and visible learning, the framework identifies four instructional configurations (Neglectful, Indulgent, Punitive, and Rigor with Support) and links them, through a set of testable propositions, to four engagement profiles (deep-agentic, strategic, surface, and disengaged). The framework is grounded in Bandura’s (1986) triadic reciprocal model, in which personal factors, observable behavior, and the instructional environment reciprocally influence one another. The analysis suggests that patterns of GenAI use cannot be understood solely in terms of technological affordances, and may be substantially shaped by the interaction between task demands, teacher commitment, and student engagement. In this context, GenAI may either support higher-order academic literacy practices or facilitate low-effort task completion, depending on the alignment between rigor and commitment. The RCAF provides a conceptual basis for examining these dynamics and offers implications for EAP pedagogy and AI policy.

items.title: Risk Management for Business Continuity
items.abstract: Ensuring business continuity in critical cyber–physical infrastructures requires a holistic risk management approach that anticipates, quantifies, and controls complex cascading effects across interdependent services. This chapter presents the solution approach developed by the DYNABIC project, which pivots around RISKM4BC , a reusable methodology and supporting tools to manage risks that affect business continuity. The approach integrates: (i) a Bow-tie Smart Center that structures threats, barriers, and consequences and is augmented with information from Large Language Models (LLMs) to enrich scenario coverage and generate mitigation recommendations; (ii) predictive business process monitoring that forecasts the performance and risk of incident response workflows; and (iii) a cascading risk model that, based on Bayesian networks, quantifies interdependent risk exposure and updates it in near real time when new evidence arrives. The methodology is operationalized through traceable risk profiles and goal-oriented aggregation that align model outputs with business objectives, as well as through user-facing views that connect live evidence to decisions. A high-level architecture describes how these components interact with monitoring and digital-twin data to maintain a live risk picture for decision making of both human operators and automated responses. A running example from transportation infrastructure (by Ferrovial) illustrates how the methodology produces actionable risk alerts (e.g., congestion likelihood and business impact level), anticipates resolution timelines, and evaluates exposure to external dependencies (e.g., power or communications). We conclude the description of the approach with methodological advantages, lessons learned, and future extensions, including business-goal linking, automated incident reporting, and interactive what-if analysis.

items.title: Scaffolding Teacher Inquiry through AI-Mediated Dialogic Reflection
items.abstract: This chapter explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated dialogic reflection as a transformative scaffold for teacher inquiry and professional learning. While reflective practice is widely recognized as foundational to teacher development, contemporary educational contexts often reduce it to solitary, checklist-driven compliance that prioritizes polished outputs over meaningful sense-making. Drawing on sociocultural theory and dialogic pedagogy, the chapter conceptualizes reflection as a socially mediated, inquiry-oriented process through which language teachers co-construct professional knowledge by engaging with multiple voices, including peers, mentors, students, academic research and classroom evidence. The chapter synthesizes research on dialogic reflection, teacher inquiry and technology-enhanced professional learning to show that reflection becomes transformative only when it is intentionally scaffolded, ethically grounded and oriented toward questioning rather than closure. Building on this foundation, the chapter examines how digital technologies and generative AI in particular can expand dialogic spaces across time and contexts. Rather than positioning AI as an authoritative source of answers, the chapter frames it as a nonauthoritative dialogic partner that supports noticing, provokes reflection, and sustains reflective continuity. The chapter concludes by proposing principled design guidelines for AI-mediated dialogic reflection that prioritize teacher agency, relational ethics, and research-oriented professionalism within broader human dialogic ecologies.

items.title: School principals’ perceptions of generative AI as a decision-support tool: implications for decisional capital
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is perceived as a decision-support mechanism in school principals’ decision-making, focusing on its perceived implications for decisional capital within a centralized education system. Design/methodology/approach Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 public school principals across different school levels in Türkiye. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify how GenAI is interpreted and positioned within principals’ decision-making processes. Findings Principals reported decision-making challenges driven by bureaucratic procedures, restricted autonomy and competing stakeholder demands. Within these constraints, GenAI was seen not as a substitute for professional judgment but as cognitive support that may improve access to information, facilitate scenario-based reasoning and inform evidence-based judgments. Principals reported varying levels of readiness to integrate GenAI into organizational decision-making, with this variation associated with digital competence, institutional support and ethical awareness. Originality/value The study extends discussions of principals’ decision-making by linking GenAI-enabled decision support to the exercise of decisional capital under centralized governance constraints, highlighting conditions under which GenAI may contribute to human-centered and ethically grounded organizational decision-making processes.

items.title: Scientific Mapping and Scientometric Evaluation of Geospatial Technologies in Landslide Research: Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Research Directions
items.abstract: Landslides remain one of the most frequent and destructive natural hazards globally, significantly influenced by climate change, rapid urbanization, deforestation, and unplanned developmental activities. In response, geospatial technologies such as Remote Sensing (RS), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and machine learning techniques have increasingly been applied to improve landslide prediction, monitoring, susceptibility mapping, and disaster risk reduction. This study presents a bibliometric evaluation of global research trends related to geospatial technologies in landslide studies during the period 2000–2025. A total of 14,909 publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus were analysed using the bibliometrix package in R. The analysis identified 2,385 publication sources and an annual scientific growth rate of 14.64%, indicating the rapid expansion of research activities in the field. The study examined publication trends, citation impact, thematic evolution, keyword structure, and international collaboration patterns. The results revealed substantial growth in scientific production, particularly after 2018, driven by advances in spatial data acquisition, artificial intelligence integration, and increasing global disaster risk awareness. China, Italy, India, and the United States emerged as the leading contributors to the research domain. Keyword and thematic analyses demonstrated a clear transition from conventional geomorphological and mapping-based approaches toward advanced machine learning-driven predictive modelling and geospatial monitoring frameworks. The study further identified two major interconnected research streams: remote sensing-based monitoring and GIS-based susceptibility modelling. The findings highlight the growing global significance, interdisciplinary nature, and technological advancement of geospatial applications in landslide research and disaster management.

items.title: SECOND LANGUAGE ACQUISITION IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE : A MULTI-PERSPECTIVE STUDY OF PERCEPTIONS
items.abstract: The acquisition of English as a second language (L2) is increasingly shaped by rapidly changing educational, social, technological, and digital environments, particularly in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). This study investigates the acquisition of English as a second language from the perspectives of students, teachers, and parents, with particular attention to the dynamic interaction of individual, familial, classroom, and technological factors. Guided by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), the study conceptualizes English language acquisition as a dynamic and interconnected process that develops through the continuous interaction of multiple contextual and individual variables. A case-study research design was employed, and purposive sampling was used to select participants from Punjab, Pakistan. The study comparatively examines patterns of convergence and divergence across these three stakeholder perspectives to develop a multidimensional understanding of English L2 acquisition in the contemporary AI-mediated learning environment. Its practical implications extend to students, parents, teachers, educational institutions, policymakers, curriculum developers, and teacher-education programmes by informing the development of more responsive and technology-integrated approaches to English language learning. Furthermore, the findings may provide insights for AI and NLP developers, digital learning designers, social-media platforms, and digital content creators to develop linguistically accessible, learner-centred, and context-sensitive English-learning resources. Overall, the study seeks to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of how multiple stakeholders perceive and experience English L2 acquisition in an increasingly AI-driven educational landscape.

items.title: Security Monitoring and Multi-Concerns Resilience Analysis
items.abstract: Critical Infrastructures (CIs) are increasingly complex cyber-physical systems whose interdependencies expose societies to cascading failures triggered by cyber and physical threats. Traditional risk assessment methods and intrusion detection systems are insufficient to address rare, high-impact, and unforeseen attacks, highlighting the need for resilience-oriented approaches that extend beyond prevention. This chapter presents AWARE4BC, a framework developed within the DYNABIC initiative to enhance CI resilience and business continuity through Digital Twin–enabled services. AWARE4BC integrates continuous infrastructure monitoring, advanced attack and anomaly detection, and holistic resilience assessment based on runtime observations. It leverages heterogeneous data sources, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and semantically enriched threat indicators to support real-time situational awareness and evidence-based decision-making. Resilience is quantified through effectiveness and resilience curves capturing degradation, absorption, recovery, and adaptation across multiple concerns, including technical, economic, environmental, and social dimensions. The framework’s practicality is validated through a hackathon-based evaluation using a transportation use case, demonstrating its ability to detect both known and zero-day attacks and assess their cascading impacts. Results confirm the added value of combining security monitoring with resilience assessment. AWARE4BC offers a generic, modular approach applicable across CI domains, contributing to more robust and adaptive protection of essential services.

items.title: Selecting Next-Generation AI Technologies for Sustainable Pharmaceutical Supply Chains: An Integrated LOPCOW–RAFSI Approach
items.abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate and prioritize next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) technologies for sustainable pharmaceutical supply chains by considering multiple technological, operational, sustainability, and regulatory criteria. Within the methodology of the study, an integrated LOPCOW–RAFSI multi-criteria decision-making framework was employed. Fifteen evaluation criteria were identified through a comprehensive literature review and reviewed for domain relevance and applicability, and six AI technology alternatives—Generative AI, Agentic AI, AI-powered Digital Twin, Federated Learning, Explainable AI, and Reinforcement Learning—were evaluated. The LOPCOW method was used to determine objective criterion weights, while the RAFSI method was applied to rank the alternatives. The findings indicate that AI-powered Digital Twin (A3) achieved the highest RAFSI score (0.666060), followed by Agentic AI (A2) (0.547032) and Explainable AI (A5) (0.541363), resulting in the overall ranking A3 > A2 > A5 > A6 > A4 > A1. The sensitivity analysis further showed that A3 retained the first position across all examined scenarios (S0–S6), although limited rank reversals occurred between A2 and A5. As a contribution to the literature, this study integrates objective weighting and robust ranking within a unified decision-support framework for evaluating emerging AI technologies and provides decision-makers with a systematic and transparent basis for prioritizing AI investments in sustainable pharmaceutical supply chains.

items.title: Selective Applicability of Deep Learning Models for Imputation of Missing Wave Observation Data: Effects of Variable Physical Characteristics and Missing-Data Patterns
items.abstract: The optimal artificial intelligence model for imputing missing wave observation data may vary according to the physical characteristics of the target variable and the missingness pattern. This study compared a temporal model, SAITS, with spatiotemporal models, GRIN, SPIN, and ImputeFormer, using 30-min interval wave observations from five stations along the southeastern coast of Korea. All models were evaluated under identical data, data-splitting, sequence, and masking conditions. Performance differences and statistical ties between model pairs were assessed using window-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. In an evaluation in which the final time step at the target station was artificially masked, SAITS yielded the lowest errors for significant wave height and significant wave period, whereas SPIN achieved the lowest angular error for wave direction, a circular variable. In the missingness-pattern sensitivity experiments, performance differences among models were generally small across random missingness rates. In contrast, under contiguous missingness within a window, GRIN achieved the best performance for both significant wave height and significant wave period when the missingness rate was at least 20%, exhibiting a pattern distinct from that observed under random missingness. Notably, under 50% contiguous missingness, GRIN was the only deep learning model that produced lower errors than linear interpolation for both significant wave height and significant wave period. These findings indicate that imputation performance may be more sensitive to the temporal continuity of missing values than to the overall missingness rate. They further suggest that exploiting spatiotemporal dependencies can be effective for reconstructing consecutive missing segments, particularly when the contiguous missingness rate exceeds 20%.

items.title: Separating Evidence from Action in AI-Assisted Procurement
items.abstract: AI-assisted procurement combines supplier observations, product matching, cost estimates and human judgments. This working paper examines how evidence, advisory outputs, eligibility checks and permission to act can be separated. A retrospective documentary case from QuickAIBuy motivates a proposed control architecture and a reproducible Boolean counterexample. Exhaustive enumeration finds advisory-dependent permission changes in three of eight paired comparisons under the deliberately coupled rule and zero under the separated rule. These are properties of an illustrative model, not measured procurement outcomes. A synthetic supplier-quote example, implementation test plan and reusable buyer review card translate the analysis into practical checks. Scope: author-approved working paper, not peer reviewed. Historical internal records were not independently rerun; no customer outcomes or production safety are established. ChatGPT assisted with synthesis, drafting, diagrams and model construction, as disclosed in the manuscript. Mohammad Maani approved the content and public deposit on 28 October 2026. items.title: Sex and Gender Differences in Disease, Pharmacotherapy, and Clinical Outcomes: Implications for Precision Medicine
items.abstract: Precision medicine hopes to make health care better by accounting for the variability of individuals' biology and clinical features in disease prediction and treatment. To achieve personalized care, however, it is essential that sex- and gender-related factors are recognized as they impact the mechanisms of disease, pharmacological actions and clinical outcomes. Disease susceptibility and response to treatment may differ between the sexes due to sex-related differences in genetics, hormones, immune regulation, epigenetic processes and metabolism; and diagnosis, access to healthcare, use of treatment and outcome may also differ across sex. There is growing evidence that considers sex and gender aspects in pharmacotherapy, discovery of biomarkers, artificial intelligence and multi-omics. Although this is starting to be recognized, there are still limitations of representation in clinical research, inconsistencies in how it is reported, and a lack of translation to clinical applications. This narrative review discusses the latest evidence regarding sex and gender differences in disease biology, pharmacotherapy, and clinical outcomes and their potential contribution to precision medicine. The incorporation of these factors into personalized health care systems can improve risk stratification, optimization of therapy, safety of drugs, and patient care.

items.title: SGTAgent: An Agent Framework for Geospatial Target Localization from Complex Spatial Semantic Queries
items.abstract: Geospatial target localization refers to determining the geographic location of targets from natural language queries, which is essential for applications such as urban management, emergency response, and location-based services. As user queries evolve from address matching toward complex forms incorporating multiple spatial semantic factors, the localization process increasingly demands the coordination of heterogeneous tools and data sources. Automation remains hindered by the lack of a unified structured representation for semantic factors, the difficulty of translating complex spatial constraints into executable operations, and the unreliability of single-round planning and execution. This study proposes SGTAgent, an agent framework for geospatial target localization from complex spatial semantic queries. The parser transforms queries into structured spatial semantic factors, the planner organizes dependent spatial workflows, and the feedback mechanism distinguishes local parameter refinement from workflow restructuring. Experiments show that SGTAgent achieves higher localization accuracy than the evaluated generic baselines across multiple LLM backbones. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, SGTAgent achieves localization accuracies of 39.86%, 68.76%, and 81.88% at distance thresholds of 100, 300, and 500 m, respectively, outperforming the evaluated agents under the corresponding experimental configurations. On complex queries using GPT-4o, it achieves an LA@500m of 80.47%, compared with 70.12% for ReAct. Ablation experiments show that removing the complete Restate–Replan feedback mechanism reduces the 500 m localization accuracy from 81.88% to 74.83%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the execution feedback mechanism under the evaluated configuration. An independent evaluation of the parser achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.76% on the original benchmark and 89.62% on independently formulated queries, indicating consistent semantic factor extraction capability across different query formulations.

items.title: Sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers: Implications for biosafety and occupational vaccination – A systematic review with meta-analysis
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta -analysis estimated the prevalence of sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers (HWW) and evaluated hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination coverage and HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, the CAPES Periodicals Portal, and Google Scholar were searched through 19 May 2026. Twenty-two studies involving approximately 9,000 HWW and 1,722 sharps injuries were included. Random-effects meta -analyses used logit transformation and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. The pooled prevalence of sharps injuries was 34.1% (95% CI, 22.8–47.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). HBV vaccination coverage was 31.1% (95% CI, 8.2–68.3%) and was not associated with sharps injury prevalence (β = 0.338; p = 0.544). Pooled HBV and HCV prevalence estimates were 2.3% (95% CI, 0.3–15.4%) and 3.36% (95% CI, 1.17–9.23%), respectively. No HCV seroconversion was reported in follow-up studies. Approximately one-third of HWW experienced sharps injuries, highlighting the need to strengthen waste segregation, personal protective equipment use, biosafety training, HBV vaccination, and occupational surveillance to improve worker safety and reduce preventable blood-borne infections.

items.title: Skills Intelligence and Skills-Based Organizing: A Bibliometric Mapping of Two Disconnected Literatures (2000–2026)
items.abstract: Skills-based organizing replaces jobs and credentials with information on skills, which artificial intelligence now extracts from job postings, résumés and human resource records at scale. Whether this information is valid for the decisions it supports depends on whether research on skills intelligence and research on human resource management inform each other. We mapped 3649 documents published between 2000 and 2026, screened with a large language model audited against a human reviewer, using co-citation, bibliographic coupling and permutation benchmarks. Managerial and computational research form separate communities: only 13% of coupling links connect them, against 46% expected by chance, and the divide is sharpest between studies of the same practice, recruitment and selection. Computational research, 71% of output in 2023–2025, is itself split between recruitment technology and labor-market analytics; it validates skill information mainly against annotated text, about one study in seven relates it to outcomes, and almost none evaluates the decisions it informs. Taxonomies such as ESCO and O*NET do not bridge the communities; work analysis does. We propose a skills intelligence value chain from data to outcomes, with five testable propositions and a research agenda for validating AI-produced skill information.

items.title: Smart Security Orchestration for the Business Continuity of Critical Infrastructures
items.abstract: Modern societies increasingly rely on critical infrastructures powered by the Internet of Things (IoT), Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), and the Digital Twin (DT) paradigm. However, their distributed and heterogeneous nature presents complex security challenges across devices, networks, and third-party integrations. This chapter introduces Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response for Business Continuity (SOAR4BC)—a core service within the DT framework designed to safeguard such infrastructures. SOAR4BC integrates Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and SOAR principles to select and execute optimal security workflows dynamically. When human oversight is needed, Chat4Operator facilitates interaction, allowing operators to approve, modify, or request alternatives. We validate SOAR4BC through real-world use cases, demonstrating its reliability and adaptability. This work highlights the potential of combining DT, DRL, and large language models (LLMs) to enhance security orchestration in IoT/CPS environments.

items.title: Smart Tourism in the Age of Social Media
items.abstract: The convergence of smart tourism technologies and social media platforms has fundamentally transformed the way travelers plan, experience, and share their journeys. This chapter examines the intersection of smart tourism ecosystems and social media dynamics through a performative travel lens, exploring how digital platforms shape tourist behavior, destination image, and the co-creation of travel experiences. Drawing on performance theory, digital sociology, and smart tourism frameworks, this chapter analyzes how it influences both individual travel decisions and broader destination marketing strategies. Smart technologies such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, big data analytics, and augmented reality are explored for their role in enabling personalized, immersive, and socially mediated tourism experiences. This chapter ultimately argues that the future of smart tourism lies not only in technological advancement but in the thoughtful integration of digital tools with human-centered, socially conscious travel values.

items.title: Social Perspective Taking and Shared Mental Model Training for Teamwork Crossing Disciplines
items.abstract: Interdisciplinary teams play a central role in solving complex scientific and operational problems, yet they frequently struggle to collaborate effectively despite high levels of technical expertise. These breakdowns often stem not only from knowledge gaps but also from difficulties interpreting collaborators’ assumptions, reasoning processes, and disciplinary perspectives. Although research on shared mental models emphasizes the importance of aligned team knowledge structures, the social-cognitive mechanisms that enable such alignment remain poorly specified. This paper argues that social perspective taking (SPT) is a foundational but under examined process linking individual understanding to team cognition. We bring together concepts from across multiple disciplines to propose a multilevel framework that reconceptualizes perspective taking as an emergent team process shaped by contextual conditions, motivational and feedback mechanisms, and interactional practices.

items.title: Social Risk Management of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: With the rapid uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, academic risks need to be viewed as not only technical issues but as socio-institutional harms that impact equity, trust, and accountability. The methodology used for this study is a conceptual literature review and qualitative synthesis of existing academic research. This study tackles the problem existing in the literature, which is unstructured definitions, by synthesizing the literature to create a complete conceptual framework for Social Risk Management (SRM). The proposed framework places SRM in a unique role, serving as the institutional interface between the introduction of AI and social outcomes, with the role of a mediator and moderator between the raw technical inputs and the negative effects of AI on society. There are four main operational pillars of SRM identified in the synthesis. This study also adds the competency of SRM as a core competency of governance, not only for its ethical dimension but also for being a proactive competency. Moreover, it offers a clear research program for future empirical studies, detailing potential ways to measure SRM and to investigate its differences in various application areas of universities, such as admissions, financial aid, tutoring, and even assessment.

items.title: Socio-economic wellness as organisational capability: a SEAM-based analysis of participation, hidden costs and governance
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explain how socio-economic wellness can become a repeatable organisational capability through participatory diagnosis, negotiated work redesign, hidden-cost translation and socio-financial governance. Design/methodology/approach A theory-building integrative review combines SEAM with organisational wellness and intervention, job-design and motivation, internal branding, equity and capability literatures. The synthesis is mechanism-based and literature-only; no company-level evidence is analysed. Findings Socio-economic wellness capability is defined as the patterned ability to detect, discuss, correct and monitor work-system dysfunctions affecting employee experience and organisational performance. The four interdependent mechanisms are conditioned by voice safety, managerial authority and resources, resource pressure, equity and governance continuity. Research limitations/implications The framework is conceptual and requires longitudinal, comparative and mixed-method testing. Future studies can operationalise its mechanisms and boundary conditions across sectors and institutional contexts. Practical implications Managers should assess wellness through operating routines: who can surface dysfunctions, whether diagnosis leads to authorised redesign, whether human consequences enter socio-economic evidence, and whether governance forums sustain learning. Social implications The framework highlights equitable access to organisational voice and influence over work conditions, extending wellness beyond programme access. Originality/value The paper differentiates socio-economic wellness capability from programmes, well-being states and organisational-health perspectives. It offers a bounded mechanism-based account of how work-system knowledge becomes authorised correction, socio-economic prioritisation and recurrent governance learning.

items.abstract: Executive Abstract: This paper examines multi-dialect stress-testing of enterprise language systems, the cross-border privacy boundarybetween Saudi PDPL, Moroccan Law 09-08 (CNDP), and European processing, and the human-oversight duties that EU AI Act Article 4 and Annex III (Section 3) place on institutional deployers. Standard English-to-Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) benchmarks mask severe operational failures when conversational agents and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines encounter authentic intra-prompt code-switching (Moroccan Darija + French, Saudi Najdi/Gulf + English, Egyptian, and Levantine). Evaluating 7 foundation models against the Arabic AI Observatory v2.0 Master Corpus (521 deterministic adversarial scenarios), we document a 37.0% accuracy degradation under dialectal negation shifts, a 2.41x token fertility infrastructure tax (1.18 vs. 2.85 tokens/word), and critical cross-border PII exfiltration vulnerabilities. Finally, we specify a zero-knowledge SHA-256 provenance protocol anchored on WaqfLedger.tech.

items.title: STARTWISE AI: AI-Based Startup Idea Validation and Franchise Recommendation System
items.abstract: Entrepreneurs often face significant challenges in evaluating startup ideas, assessing business feasibility, identifying potential risks, and selecting suitable franchise opportunities due to limited access to structured market information and expert guidance. This paper presents STARTWISE AI, an AI-based decision-support framework designed to assist aspiring entrepreneurs in startup idea validation and personalized franchise recommendation. The proposed framework integrates machine learning, data analytics, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to provide structured insights into early-stage business opportunities. The startup validation module analyzes user-provided information, including business domain, target audience, estimated investment, geographical location, and business objectives, to support feasibility assessment and identify potential risk factors. Machine learning techniques can be incorporated to estimate business viability, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) can be used to interpret model predictions by identifying the relative contributions of input features. In addition, the franchise recommendation module matches user preferences, investment capacity, industry interests, and location requirements with relevant franchise opportunities. The framework is designed using React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the frontend, Python and FastAPI for backend services, and Neon PostgreSQL for data storage. STARTWISE AI aims to improve the accessibility, interpretability, and organization of preliminary entrepreneurial decision-making. By combining startup assessment with personalized franchise discovery, the framework provides a unified platform for exploring business opportunities. The system is intended to support, rather than replace, professional market research and financial evaluation. Its practical effectiveness must be established through appropriate experiments, comparative evaluation, and user testing. Keywords— Startup Idea Validation, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, SHAP, Franchise Recommendation System, Business Feasibility Analysis, Decision Support System..

items.title: STELLAR: Large Language Model Enhanced Spatiotemporal Semantic Fusion for Urban Next POI Recommendation
items.abstract: Urban next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation is fundamental to location-based services, yet accurate prediction remains challenging because user trajectories are sparse, semantically incomplete, and tightly constrained by time and geography. Recent graph and Transformer models capture transition regularities, while language model-based recommenders introduce textual knowledge, but these two lines of work remain weakly coupled: semantic priors may be plausible in language space yet infeasible under a user’s actual mobility state, and purely behavioral encoders fail to infer latent intent when observations are scarce. We introduce STELLAR, a unified state transition framework that treats language knowledge as a calibrated prior rather than an independent prediction branch. STELLAR first induces semantic mobility priors from structured trajectory descriptions, then projects them into a shared transition state and learns a feasibility gate conditioned on spatial reachability, temporal rhythm, and both short- and long-term behavioral context. A transition memory subsequently propagates this calibrated state to candidate POIs, allowing semantic evidence to influence prediction only when it is consistent with executable mobility. This design directly addresses semantic-behavioral misalignment and avoids ad hoc late fusion. Across three public check-in benchmarks, STELLAR consistently outperforms both purely behavioral and language-augmented baselines in ranking accuracy, robustness to corrupted trajectories, and cold-start generalization.
